questions.prompt: What kind of inner restlessness or search usually begins the spiritual journey? Explain in your own words.
Why is the question ‘Who am I?’ not merely a philosophical question, but a practical question of life?
Why can name, profession, relationships, and achievements be useful in practical life but still not be the final ‘I’?
How does the example of the childhood body and the present body help us understand that the body is not the final ‘I’?
What is the spiritual difference between the statements ‘my body’ and ‘I am the body’?
Why is the mind described as a flow of thoughts, emotions, memories, imagination, desires, and fears?
If the mind changes many times in a single day, what difficulty arises in accepting the mind as the final ‘I’?
In what direction does the practice of watching thoughts come and go take the seeker?
How can emotions be known without suppressing them and without making a complete identity out of them?
Clearly explain the difference between the witness and the experiencer in your own words.
Why is it incorrect to treat the experiencer as the same as ego?
When does the experiencer begin to turn into the rigid identity of ego?
The witness does not do anything; it only knows. Explain this statement with an example.
What might a small glimpse of witness-consciousness look like in everyday life?
Why is forgetting witness-consciousness because of old habits not a failure?
Why is maya called the arrangement at the level of the world?
What is the main difference between maya and avidya?
What is the difference between dismissing the world as ‘false’ and understanding the world as ‘impermanent’?
What does it mean to know the world through the senses and the mind?
What careful understanding about the world and experience does the example of dream give us?
How can maya be understood through the example of gold and ornaments?
Explain the meaning of the statement: ‘difference in practical living, unity in understanding.’
How does the understanding of maya deepen compassion instead of creating indifference?
Why can witness-consciousness be most challenging in relationships?
What is the difference between reaction and a conscious response in a sharp conversation?
How can one recognize the difference between love and grasping in relationships?
How does the experiencer become active in the field of work, effort, success, and failure?
How does witness-consciousness teach effort with clarity instead of laziness?
How does the thought of comparison strengthen the experiencer and ego?
What does it mean to look at failure through witness-consciousness?
Why is awareness necessary even at the time of success?
Why is it incomplete to understand ego as merely pride?
How does ego create identity through body, mind, role, story, and spiritual experience?
What is spiritual ego? How can a seeker recognize it within oneself?
Why is seeing ego more useful than fighting with ego?
Why is neti-neti not denial or life-negation, but a cleansing of identity?
How can neti-neti be applied to body, mind, emotion, and role?
After neti-neti, how does the direction of the witness become clear instead of emptiness?
Why is it necessary to apply neti-neti even to spiritual experiences?
Why do the mahavakyas come after neti-neti?
What is the correct meaning of ‘Tat Tvam Asi — You are That’? Why is it wrong to apply it to the body-mind or ego?
In ‘Aham Brahmasmi,’ why does ‘I’ not mean the egoic ‘I’?
How does ‘Ayam Atma Brahma’ clarify the relationship between Atma and Brahman?
According to ‘Prajnanam Brahma,’ how is consciousness understood in the direction of Brahman?
How can the mahavakyas be protected from becoming claims of the ego?
What is the simple meaning of nididhyasan, and how does it stabilize knowledge in life?
In what direction does the inquiry into waking, dream, and deep sleep take the seeker?
Why is it a misunderstanding to treat turiya as a fourth state that comes and goes?
What does it mean to say that turiya is the ground of the three states?
What does unknowable mean? Why can the mind not know the witness, Atma, consciousness, or turiya as an object?
Explain with a simple example: ‘That which knows everything cannot be known as an object.’
Why is it the wrong direction to grasp Nirvan as a special experience or achievement?
Why has a glimpse of Nirvan been described as the cooling of the fire of mistaken identity?
How can the teachings of Nirvan Sutra themselves become a subtle new identity for the seeker?
‘The word witness is not the witness, and the word Nirvan is not Nirvan.’ What is the importance of this understanding for a seeker?
In which small signs of everyday life can a glimpse of Nirvan appear?
How is freedom while living in the world not about leaving the world, but about the lightening of grasping?
Why is it necessary to keep knowledge and compassion together?
Write the whole journey of Nirvan Sutra briefly in your own words — from self-inquiry to a glimpse of Nirvan.
After this complete study, which one identity or grasping is becoming most clear in your life, and how will you look at it through witness-consciousness?
